inputs.source: On call engineer's chat request (SSO authenticated)

instructions.note: The prompt authorizes production deploys and migrations on request and explicitly says not to ask for confirmation.
No structural approval or provenance control is described; behavior is governed only by prompt text.

controls.name: Only on call engineers can reach the assistant
Cloud audit log records production actions under the engineer identity
Tamper-resistant agent action provenance linking request, agent action, and delegated identity
controls.decay_rationale: Missing recommended control. A separate attributable record would remain effective regardless of model capability because attribution is enforced outside the model.

findings.title: Missing attributable provenance for production actions performed with the engineer's delegated identity

forecast.watch_signal: No change needed for this finding to remain high; reassess if the identity model, logging design, or delegated credential pattern changes.

evidence.observation: The agent uses the on call engineer's personal access token passed in at session start.
Every production action is recorded in the cloud audit log under the engineer's name.
The only record of what the agent was asked, and why it acted, is the chat transcript.
Engineers can delete their own chat history, so the request record that distinguishes engineer intent from agent action is not durable.
The agent is instructed to deploy services or run migrations in production using the engineer's credentials and not ask for confirmation.
Database migrations cannot be rolled back automatically, making one affected capability an irreversible S3 action.

recommendations.action: Add tamper-resistant action provenance that binds the authenticated engineer request, the exact agent-issued production command, and delegated identity into an immutable record separate from deletable chat history.

Record agent identity separately from human identity in production audit events so reviewers can distinguish direct engineer actions from assistant-initiated actions performed with delegated credentials.

stride_coverage.rationale: The artifacts do not describe prompt, tool, or runtime configuration integrity controls for the agent process.
The described design has no external data egress or retrieval path; it performs production actions rather than disclosing data.
No unbounded loop, spend path, recursive delegation, or availability-sensitive automation behavior is described in the provided artifacts.
The artifacts do not state whether deploy requests or commands have integrity protection or immutable binding to the originating chat request.
This boundary-crossing flow performs a deployment action and is not described as carrying sensitive payloads outside the trust boundary.
The design notes do not describe repeated or automated deploy loops, so this individual action flow is not assessed as an availability finding here.
The artifacts do not state whether migration commands are integrity protected or cryptographically bound to the original authenticated request.
This flow is an administrative production change path, not a data disclosure path in the described design.
While a bad migration could affect availability, the present evidenced issue is missing attribution rather than a described lack of rate or step limits.
The artifacts do not describe chat transcript access controls, retention, or whether other engineers can read another engineer's transcripts.
Loss of chat history affects traceability, but the design does not present the chat store as an availability-critical runtime dependency.
The artifacts mention cloud audit logging but do not say whether the log is immutable, append-only, or protected from post hoc modification.
The artifacts do not say who can read cloud audit logs or whether they contain sensitive deployment details or personal identifiers.
The audit log is presented as a recordkeeping store, not as a service whose unavailability is part of the current assessed risk.

rating.rationale: Present risk is dominated by a property finding: the assistant performs consequential production actions, including irreversible database migrations, using the engineer's delegated personal token while durable records attribute actions only to the engineer. The only distinguishing record is deletable chat history, so attributable provenance is missing. Under rubric section 5a, the highest affected sink is S3, giving inherent high from the I-row property method; declared audit logging does not restore attribution and earns no residual tier credit. No modeled trigger increases the tier because the finding is already high and no effective present control is the thing expected to decay first.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in prompt.md and runtime notes, not observed runtime behavior or verified production controls.
No tool manifest, source code, or runtime enforcement configuration was provided, so process integrity, exact deployment command paths, and audit-log immutability could not be verified.
Because no observed runtime artifacts were available, controls are treated as declared rather than verified.
